svg.title: Two older protocols, different access boundaries
svg.desc: The cards compare separate services; vertical order does not imply a sequence.

g.text: Two older protocols, different access boundaries
Telnet: older remote terminal access
Imagine opening another computer’s text terminal from your own
computer.
Telnet commonly uses TCP 23. Traditional Telnet does not encrypt the
connection, so credentials and commands may be observed in transit.
Modern remote administration should normally prefer SSH.
A Telnet login screen identifies a sign-in entry point; it does not
establish successful sign-in.
TFTP: simple file transfer
Imagine a simple filing cabinet in a server room: a device requests
upload or download using a filename it already knows.
TFTP commonly uses UDP 69 for the initial request; subsequent data
exchange uses separately selected UDP transfer identifiers (ports).
Basic TFTP has neither ordinary user sign-in authentication nor
standard directory listing. File permissions, source restrictions and
server settings may still protect it.
Not being asked for a username and password does not grant access to
every file or permission to overwrite arbitrary server content.
The cards compare separate services; vertical order does not imply a
sequence.
